source.title: Lazy vs hasty: linearization in deep networks impacts learning schedule based on example difficulty
source.authors: Thomas George; Guillaume Lajoie; A. Baratin

record.file_problem: Full paper text provided, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests fitting noisy labels in a feature-learning versus linearized regime, refining the claim: learning noisy labels is delayed while clean patterns are learned, and the dynamics and generalization differ by regime. It does not test fitting a completely random labeling of the entire training set.
record.gate_note: The label-noise experiment flips 15% of CIFAR10 training labels and measures clean, noisy, and test losses/accuracies over training. Other reported C-score and spurious-feature results concern example-learning schedules, not random-label fitting. Figure-only values are not reconstructed. Cited results from prior studies are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study directly tests V6 through clean-versus-noisy learning trajectories in feature-learning and linearized networks. Both regimes learn clean examples before memorizing corrupted labels; their relative prioritization differs. This supports and extends V6 rather than demonstrating a failure of it.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors conclude that feature-learning dynamics prioritize easy examples more strongly than lazy dynamics. With label noise, both regimes learn clean examples first, but the nonlinear regime delays noisy-label memorization further relative to clean-learning progress and attains a better best test loss. The comparisons are normalized by training progress, rather than establishing a larger fraction of elapsed training time.
record.recipe_differences: Compares standard feature-learning training (α = 1) with a deliberately linearized copy (α = 100) using a scaling procedure; tests partial label noise rather than fully random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: The learning schedule differs between α = 1 and α = 100; for the noisy-label experiment, the reported memorization phase begins at clean-example loss 1.25 versus 1.5, respectively. Appendix E reports that varying learning rate with α = 1 did not reproduce the divergence attributed to α scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed 15% corruption, feature-learning training attains lower best test loss than linearized training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature learning can improve best achievable generalization under partial label noise relative to lazy training.

record.problems: The label-noise evidence shown is for one 15% corruption level and a reported run; the text provides qualitative comparisons rather than numerical endpoint values or uncertainty estimates. The study does not test wholly random labels or the other claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. C-score, toy-dataset, and spurious-correlation results were not extracted because they do not measure any of the listed claim versions; values visible only in plots were not reconstructed.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test error, and preservation of the original training recipe.
Relative time to fit true versus completely random labels, and convergence changes across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit across corruption fractions and steadily increasing test error toward chance. A single 15% corruption condition and between-regime test-loss comparison do not test this relationship.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting, and generalization after removing them.
Learning dynamics under completely random labeling and across a range of corruption fractions.

missing.what: VGG11 label-noise replication and ResNet18 runs varying initialization and minibatch order are unrecorded conditions relevant to the robustness of V6. Extract their qualitative trajectories where readable; do not infer numerical endpoints from extracted axes.

The accuracy-based confirmation explicitly states that nonlinear training starts memorizing noisy examples later than linearized training. This provides a behavioral measure alongside the loss trajectories.
missing.locator: Appendix F; Figure 11, left panel and caption.

missing.what: The unconstrained two-layer MLP reproduces clean-first label-noise dynamics on the synthetic dataset. The record incorrectly excludes all toy results as unrelated to the claim versions.
missing.locator: Appendix G; Figure 14 middle panel and caption; Section 4.4 Example 2.

missing.what: Learning-rate controls at α = 1 span 0.01, 0.003, 0.0001, and 0.000001; their normalized noisy-example trajectories remain similar during early training. This control bears on whether the observed learning schedule is merely a learning-rate artifact.

record.verdict_notes: Remove both proposed limits_scope verdicts: untested corruption fractions and missing perfect-fit endpoints are coverage gaps, not observed failures. Additional architectures and seed checks are reported, so describing the entire evidence as a single run is incomplete. Exact appendix curve values cannot be recovered reliably from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment assigns completely random labels to the entire training set or tests zero/near-zero training error and chance test error under the original architecture and hyperparameters.
No constant-factor comparison of training time to fit wholly random labels; no sweep over the fraction of corrupted labels.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment.
Tests only one corruption level (15%), not a sweep from none to all; does not establish a steady rise of test error toward chance or perfect training fit throughout.
Does not test weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation as barriers to random-label fitting or their removal's effect on true-label generalization.

Tests 15% randomly flipped labels, with clean versus noisy example losses over training; does not test completely random labels or establish the same sequence across other corruption rates and models.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR10 with 15% of training examples assigned a wrong random label; tracked clean-label and noisy-label losses through training.
rows.measure: Training loss on clean examples and on noisy examples over training; onset of noisy-label memorization relative to clean-example loss.
rows.baseline: Linearized run at α = 100, compared at equal clean-example loss.
rows.value: The study states that a first phase learns examples with true labels while loss on wrong-label examples increases; a second phase starts at 1.25 clean examples loss in the non-linear run, where random labels are getting memorized.
rows.note: One reported run/condition; the paper describes a qualitative phase sequence and gives the non-linear onset point, but no numerical training-error endpoint.
rows.check: The reported clean-first, noise-later sequence directly matches V6, so partial is inappropriate. Remove V4: this trajectory at one corruption rate does not measure perfect training fit or degradation across noise fractions. Specify that batch normalization is omitted.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2.2; Figure 2 caption and following paragraph; Appendix C.2.

rows.subject: ResNet18

rows.baseline: Non-linear run at α = 1, compared at equal clean-example loss.

rows.check: The linearized run also exhibits the full sequence described by V6. Remove V4. The stated learning rate 0.01 is the base rate; at α = 100 the effective rate is 0.000001 under the paper's scaling. Batch normalization is omitted.
